analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the doubled estate and gift tax exemption for the largest inheritances.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote, so the larger estate tax exemption remains temporary and is set to shrink after 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 tax law (Public Law 115-97) temporarily doubled the estate and gift tax exemption from $5 million to $10 million per person, but only for deaths and gifts between 2018 and the end of 2025. This bill would write the doubled $10 million exemption into permanent law, so the very largest estates would never again owe tax on the first $10 million of value per person. Because it amends the underlying tax code rather than the temporary provision, the change would take effect for deaths and gifts after 2017. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and received no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Only estates and gifts above the exemption amount benefit, and those amounts are per person, so a married couple could shield $20 million. The exemption is indexed for inflation, so the benefit compounds over time. Estates below the exemption already pay nothing, so the change matters exclusively for the very wealthiest households and their heirs, who would keep up to 40 cents of tax on each dollar above the threshold. Wealth planners and estate attorneys also gain from a permanent rule they can plan around, rather than one scheduled to expire.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The wealthiest households and their heirs

how_it_helps.text: Writes the $10 million per-person estate and gift tax exemption (indexed for inflation) permanently into the tax code, replacing the temporary provision that expires after 2025
Applies retroactively to deaths and gifts after December 31, 2017, matching the window the 2017 tax law set
Removes the expiration date by striking the provision that reverts the exemption to $5 million, so estates of any size above the exemption would face tax only beyond the doubled threshold

analysis.who_pays: Federal tax revenue: the estate tax currently raises tens of billions of dollars a year, nearly all from estates above roughly $11 million per person. Making the doubled exemption permanent would forgo that revenue permanently, either adding to deficits or requiring other taxes or spending cuts to offset it. Since most families pay no estate tax at all, the cost falls on general taxpayers in the form of higher debt or foregone public revenue, while the gain is concentrated in a small number of very large estates.

drawbacks.text: The benefit is entirely concentrated: only estates above the doubled exemption pay any estate tax, so making the increase permanent is a large tax cut for a few thousand of the largest estates each year and no cut for nearly everyone else

It is a permanent revenue loss: the 2017 law deliberately made the doubled exemption temporary so it would cost less over ten years, and this bill would remove that expiration, locking in the forgone revenue indefinitely
The bill has no revenue offsets and no companion cost estimate in the record, so its full budget cost would fall on deficits or require offsetting cuts elsewhere

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain goes to a narrow group — heirs of estates worth more than $10 million per person — while the cost is a permanent loss of federal revenue that affects everyone through deficits or offsetting taxes and cuts. The estate tax touches so few families that ordinary households would see no direct benefit, only the fiscal consequences. On balance, this is a one-directional transfer to the largest inheritances.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2018, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Kenny Marchant introduced the bill on June 26, 2018, to make the doubled $10 million estate and gift tax exemption permanent
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which was its only action
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action followed, and the bill attracted no cosponsors
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill expired with the committee referral as its sole action

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: General taxpayers and federal revenue came out ahead: the doubled exemption, which is scheduled to shrink after 2025 under the 2017 tax law's sunset, was not made permanent, so the revenue from the very largest estates remains on the books. The bill's intended beneficiaries — heirs of the largest estates — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; the estate tax sunset survives

for.name: Rep. Kenny Marchant
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the doubled estate and gift tax exemption permanent; it was his committee's jurisdiction and he pursued it no further in the record

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 26, 2018 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one else took a position: the bill had one Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no recorded opposition, so no party line can be measured.

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates (households above the exemption)
industries.note: Because the bill died, the doubled $10 million exemption stays temporary and is scheduled to revert to the pre-2018 level after 2025, leaving very large estates exposed to up to 40% tax above the threshold. The bill would have shielded the first $10 million per person permanently; its failure preserves that revenue.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory industry
industries.note: A permanent, higher exemption would have simplified long-term planning, but the temporary-then-expiring structure of the 2017 tax law keeps demand for complex trust and planning work alive as 2026 approaches. Practitioners benefit from uncertainty their clients pay for.

The estate tax continues to collect revenue almost entirely from estates above roughly $11 million per person. Keeping the sunset intact avoids a permanent revenue loss that would otherwise be made up through deficits or other taxes.
